_source: Every job on this board was written for this board. The QUESTIONS are the exception to nothing: each one is answered by a sentence that is already published on the page the marker sits on, and each was read off that page before it was written here rather than remembered. Where a question asks for a person's name it is a name our own page already credits -- Barad, Oldaker, Schaber, Thornburg, Lee and Duffy -- because a quiz that made somebody guess at an attribution would be teaching the opposite of the habit this street kept.
_codes: One word, A-Z, typed case-insensitively with spaces and punctuation ignored. A word rather than a random string because a word can be said out loud, remembered across a walk to another room, and typed by somebody who finds typing expensive. These are not secrets and the board does not pretend they are: the code is printed in the room's own markup, on a public page, and anybody who wants to read the source can have the lot. The board holds a checksum instead of the plain word purely so that View Source on ONE page is not a spoiler sheet for every room. That is a courtesy, not a lock, and make-guild.py says so where it computes it.
_no_score: There is no tally here, no percentage, no streak, no rank you climb and nothing that expires. The board stamps a job when you hand its code in and that is the whole of the bookkeeping. This is the pebbling cabinet's refusal arriving in the one room on the street most likely to talk itself out of it -- a job board is EXACTLY the shape of thing that grows a score, and a score beside a Disabled people's walking tour would quietly turn a wander into a workload. make-guild.py refuses the vocabulary.
_class: The difficulty class is HOW FAR YOU WALK, not how clever you are. I is on the street, II is through a door off a room, III is off the street altogether -- the field past the treeline at one end, the road past the last streetlight at the other, or the caverns underneath. III IS NOT THREE CLASSES AND THERE IS NO IV OR V: the edges are different directions rather than different distances -- one is not even along the street, it is down -- and numbering them would invent an ordering nobody walks. Nothing about the class says anything about the person doing it, which is the whole reason it is defined by geography and enumerated in the tool rather than typed per job.

hints: The room says it in three words, near the readings.
It is the reason a library lends a book rather than giving it away.
The author is living, publishing, and narrated the real audiobook herself.
It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first.
It is pitch 02, the meadow with the path through it.
Low in the grass at the very bottom of the meadow, below the clearing.
quests.learned: That room also carries a correction to our own glossary near the top rather than in a footnote: two of our entries attribute a phrase to Barry Lopez that he never wrote. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins.

quests.title: The fourth learning space
quests.posted: There is a sunflower head drying on a hook outside the hermitage at pitch 03. Three of the four primordial learning spaces are laid out inside that cabin. The fourth is not in there, and the room will tell you where it is.
quests.takes: three minutes, and some reading
quests.target: a sunflower head, drying

ask.question: Cave, campfire and watering hole are in the cabin. Name the fourth. One word.
ask.why: The three zones are David Thornburg's primordial learning spaces, and the room names them as his. There is a fourth, and the room says out loud that it is not in there — it is the door you came in by, where you go and make something out of what the other three gave you.
hints: The room says out loud that the fourth one is not in the cabin.
It is the door you came in by.
Four letters.
It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first.
It is pitch 03, the cabin on wheels with the panels on the roof.
At the very bottom of the page, below the last of the cabin.
quests.learned: It is the only room on this street lit by morning. Every other world here is a dark ground with light applied to it; a cabin that runs on the sun and reads as midnight would be an argument against itself.

quests.title: The two habits that survived
quests.posted: There is a colophon mark at the foot of the liner notes. This street dropped most of the care its sibling sites run on and kept exactly two things. Name the one that is not contrast.
quests.takes: two minutes, and some reading
quests.target: a colophon mark

ask.question: Two habits survived onto this street. One is contrast. What is the other? One word.
ask.why: It is a licence rather than a house style, it is the cheapest thing on the page, and it is the only one of our habits whose absence is a legal problem rather than an aesthetic one. So the credits got louder instead of going away.
hints: It is the thing this whole page is.
It is a licence rather than a house style.
Eleven letters, and it begins with an A.
It is one of the pages linked from the pavement at the foot of the street.
Go to the very bottom of the credits.
At the very bottom of the page, below the last credit.
quests.learned: Contrast survived for a reason that is not the obvious one. This is a Disabled people's organisation, and a glitter-maximalist site that excluded the people it is for would be a self-own of exactly the kind we exist to name. The fix was never to tone it down — it was the dial.

quests.title: What a spider's best answer is
quests.posted: Somebody has dropped a blank plant label on the path in the garden, which is through the gate in the wall between two of the shopfronts. Pick it up. While you are in there, settle what that room says the garden spider is for, because it is careful about it and the sentence is worth carrying back out with you.
quests.takes: two or three minutes, most of it one paragraph
quests.target: a blank wooden plant label

ask.question: The garden says what a spider's best answer is, in our own words. One word.
ask.why: Grounding the spider in our own garden changes where its answers come from and not whether they can be wrong, so every trail it puts somebody on ends at a page a person wrote. What it is genuinely good at is the step before the word: taking "why does switching tasks hurt" and getting somebody to the glossary entry, the pattern or the recipe. It is the way in rather than the thing itself.
hints: It is in the room's own writing about the spider, not on the button.
The sentence is about what a spider is FOR: a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it.
The room says a spider's best answer is an entrance.
It is not behind a shopfront. There is a gate in the wall between two of them, down past the noticeboard.
Through the gate is the garden, where every bed is one of the other sites we publish.
Right at the foot of the garden, on the path below the hedge and the dial.
quests.learned: A glossary exists to give somebody a word for an experience that usually goes unnamed, and a tool that can route them from the experience to the word is doing that job one step earlier. What it must never do is stand in for the page at the other end, which is why that room says out loud that it can be wrong and links the ethics pages where we hold the line.

quests.title: Which printing it was
quests.posted: There is a shopfront on the street with a commonplace book left open on the desk in it. A nib has been put down beside the book. Pick it up, and while you are there settle the question the whole room turns on: one of the quotations in that book had to be traced to a particular printing before it could go in, because the obvious guess was wrong.
quests.takes: two or three minutes, most of it one list
quests.target: a steel nib laid down beside the book

ask.question: The Emily Dickinson line in that book is not in the series everybody assumes. Which series is it in? One word.
ask.why: It is in the Second Series of 1891, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson, not the first. That is the whole argument of the room in one entry: a title is not a source, these texts differ between printings, and the only thing that told anybody which one it was was going and reading the title page above the poem instead of remembering. Todd and Higginson edited Dickinson's punctuation before they let her out, so the printing you name decides the words you are quoting.
hints: It is not on the card with the quotation on it. It is in the room's list of what the book will and will not do.
The rule is the one about naming the printing rather than the title, and the room calls this entry its proof.
The room says it is in the second series, not the first.
It is a shopfront on the street, with the only pale window in the row.
The book is open on a desk, and the nib is down at the foot of the page.
Below the attribution slip, at the bottom of the room.
quests.learned: Naming the printing is not pedantry, it is the difference between quoting somebody and quoting somebody's editor. A quotation that names only its title cannot be checked by anybody, which is how a misquotation travels for a century in perfectly good faith.

quests.title: The words are not in the hole
quests.posted: There is a shaft at the end of the street with seven recordings hanging in it, all of them of one song or of the record that song came out of. Go down it and count the lyrics.
quests.takes: a couple of minutes, and longer if you press something
quests.target: an engraver's block on the shaft wall
hints: It is a storefront on the street, not behind another room.
The marker is on the wall of the shaft like everything else in there — keep going down past the engravings, the presses and the trail.
Right at the foot of the page, under the dial.

ask.question: Seven recordings of one song, and our own glossary entry prints the whole lyric. How many lines of it are printed in this room? One word.
ask.why: None of it. Our glossary entry has the words; this room deliberately does not. Song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not — music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel. It is the same reasoning that makes the Zibaldone refuse a song outright. So the recordings are offered instead, with Grace Slick's own published account of writing it, and a generator refuses a lyric field rather than leaving it to anybody's care — because the room reads thinner without the words, and somebody will eventually be tempted to help.
hints: Look at what is actually printed between the buttons. Not the titles — the verse.
The room says it out loud twice: once under that section's heading and once in the house rules.
It is a number, and it is the smallest one there is.

quests.learned: A room can carry a recording without carrying the words to it, and the difference is a legal one rather than a matter of taste. It is also the one place on this street where a room deliberately does less than the page it was built from.

quests.title: What the server says instead of no
quests.posted: There is a save room on the street with a bed in it and no monsters. It is numbered after an HTTP status code, and that status code has a companion that turns a refusal into a time. Go and find out what the companion is called.
quests.takes: a couple of minutes, and as long as you like after that
quests.target: a pillow on the floor at the foot of the bed
hints: It is a storefront on the street, not behind another room — although there is also a back stair up to it from this board.
The room explains its own number in a section of its own. The answer is a header name, and it is printed in bold there.
Right at the foot of the page, under the dial.

ask.question: Room 429 is named after 429 Too Many Requests. What is the header a server sends alongside it to say when to come back? One word, hyphen and all.
ask.why: Retry-After. A 400 says you made a mistake, a 403 says you are not allowed and a 500 says something inside has fallen over — but a 429 says only that the rate is wrong, and a rate is a property of a situation rather than of a person. Retry-After is the part that makes it kind: not a refusal, a time. Which is why the room hands out five of them as slips you can send somebody, and why it is crip time with a header name.
hints: It is in the section called Why the room is numbered 429, in the last paragraph.
Two words joined by a hyphen, and the second one is a preposition.
It begins with Retry.

quests.learned: A status code can be a kindness. 429 is the one thing a computer says that blames a rate rather than a person, and the header beside it turns a no into a when — which is most of what anybody at capacity is actually trying to say.

quests.title: The letter that is a hole
quests.posted: There is a type foundry on the street. Its own nameplate is set in a face that is not drawn the way the others are, and the room explains what it is instead. Go and read the two paragraphs about it.
quests.takes: a few minutes, and a long time after that if you start pulling proofs
quests.target: a single piece of type lying on the workshop floor
hints: A shopfront on the street, between the save room and the empty one.
The room has a short section about its own display face, under the bench and the proof.
Right at the foot of the page, under the dial.

ask.question: This room is set in a stencil, and it says a stencil letter is not a mark. What is it instead? One word.
ask.why: A hole. A stencil letter is cut OUT of a sheet of metal so it can be used again and come out the same every time, which is the whole idea of type arriving four hundred years early and in the wrong material. It is also why a stencil has bridges across its letters: without them the counter — the enclosed space inside an o or an a — would simply fall out of the sheet. Nobody cutting punches or drawing outlines has that problem, and no other face on this street has that shape.
hints: It is in the section called Why this room is set in a stencil, in the first paragraph, in bold.
Four letters, and the opposite of a mark.
It is what a counter would fall out of.

quests.learned: A letterform can be shaped by what it is cut into rather than by what anybody wanted it to look like. The bridges across a stencil are not styling: they are the only thing holding the middle of the letter in.

quests.title: The joke in the street's own name
quests.posted: This street is named after somebody and the name is a pun in two languages. There is a page about it, reached from a line under the dial on the front page rather than through any door. Go and find out who the joke is about.
quests.takes: five minutes, or twenty if you read the whole history
quests.target: a drain in the gutter
hints: Not behind a door. It is linked from the front page, in the paragraph under the loudness dial.
The page has a section called Where Danny came from, and the answer is in the paragraph that begins with the word pun.
Right at the foot of the page, under the dial.

ask.question: Danny the Street is named after a drag performer whose stage surname is French for “the street”. What is that surname? Two words or one, either is fine.
ask.why: La Rue — Danny La Rue, the drag performer, whose stage surname is the French “la rue”, the street. So the character is a female impersonator who is also a literal thoroughfare, and the place and the person cannot be separated out from each other for tidying. That is the joke the whole of this site is built on top of.
hints: It is in the section called Where Danny came from, in the paragraph about the pun.
Two short French words, and the first one is the definite article.
The performer's first name was Danny too.

quests.learned: The street you are standing on is named after a drag performer by way of a French pun, which means the architecture of this site — rooms that refuse to match, and a street that rearranges itself for whoever turns up — was somebody else's idea first and is credited rather than quietly absorbed.

quests.title: The far end of the street
quests.posted: The street has two edges. Everybody finds the field past the treeline; far fewer walk the other way, out past the last streetlight, where the kerb gives up and becomes a verge. Go and read the road, and find out what is actually lighting it.
quests.takes: five minutes, and there is nothing to press
quests.target: a reflector set into the verge
hints: It is not on the street. Leave by the far end rather than the treeline end — the link is under the shopfronts, past the noticeboard and the gate.
The answer is in the list at the top of the road, in the item about how far you can see.
Right at the foot of the road, under the section about the unlit signs.

ask.question: The Outskirts says you can only see a certain distance, and it is very specific about what is doing the lighting. What light is it?
ask.why: Headlights — low, level, close, and coming from off the page, which is why every sign out there has a bright face and no back, and why the road goes black an inch past the beam. It is the one light no other world on this street uses, and it is the whole reason the area can say it is always dark without simply being unreadable: what the beam reaches, it reaches properly.
hints: It is in the first item of the list called What is out here.
It is not the moon and it is not a lamp. There are no lamps out there; that is the point of the place.
You are in a car, and you have stopped.

quests.learned: The street has an edge at each end and they are not the same kind of edge — a field you walk into at one, a road you drive out of at the other — which is also why the guild's class III stopped saying past the treeline and started naming both.

quests.title: What the band did without
quests.posted: Down the first turning off The Outskirts there is a drive-in screen standing in black water, and an appreciation of the band it is named after. That appreciation makes a point of something the band deliberately did not have, for years, on purpose. Go and find out what.
quests.takes: ten minutes, or an hour if you start pressing the records
quests.target: a window speaker on a post
hints: It is off the street — out past the last streetlight, then the first turning.
The answer is in the appreciation at the top, in the short paragraph that is entirely about a thing that was missing.
Right at the foot of the room, under the rack of records.

ask.question: The appreciation says The Cramps deliberately did without one instrument for years. Which one?
ask.why: The bass — two guitars, a drum kit, and a deliberate hole where the bottom end goes, which is why an early Cramps record sounds like something coming through a wall rather than off a stage. It is a limitation chosen on purpose and then defended for a decade, and that is a more useful noise than it sounds if you have ever been told that the thing you manage without is the thing you need.
hints: It is the paragraph that starts by saying there was no one of these.
It is the instrument that normally holds down the bottom end of a band.
Two guitars and drums, and nothing underneath them.

quests.learned: A band can remove the part everybody treats as structural and keep going for thirty years, and the missing piece becomes the sound rather than a fault in it.

quests.title: The tree nobody will cut
quests.posted: Second turning off the road out of town there is a ring of earth standing in a field, and one kind of tree growing on it that people across a whole country decline to touch. A motorway was moved rather than fell one. Go and find out which tree.
quests.takes: ten minutes, and there is nothing to press out there
quests.target: a sprig of thorn on the bank
hints: It is off the street — past the last streetlight, then the second turning.
The answer is in the documented half of the page, the part about earthworks rather than the part about rules.
Right at the foot of the room, under the section about why the door is not opened.

ask.question: Sithen names one kind of tree that is left standing on a fairy fort, and that stopped a motorway in County Clare in 1999. Which tree?
ask.why: The whitethorn — hawthorn, sceach — which the tradition is specific about: cutting the thorn growing on a ring was reputed to be the death of whoever did it, and in 1999 a campaign led by the folklorist Eddie Lenihan saved one at Latoon from being felled for the M18. It is still there. The reason that is in a room on this site is the comparison it invites: a whole country will make an enormous, permanent, expensive accommodation on the strength of this matters and I am not going to justify it, and the same country will ask a Disabled person for a letter before it moves a desk.
hints: It is in the list of documented facts, and it is named twice — once for the taboo and once for the motorway.
It has two common English names and an Irish one, and any of them will do.
The first half of the word is a colour.

quests.learned: There is a tree in Ireland that a motorway was routed around, and the paperwork for that accommodation was a shrug — which is worth holding next to what is usually asked of a Disabled person before anything gets moved.

quests.title: Counsel, not commandment
quests.posted: There is a kitchen on this street with the good china out and not one cup matching the next. One of the things laid on that table is famous, and the word at the front of it is the whole reason it never hardened into a rule. Go and find out what that word means.
quests.takes: ten minutes, and the kettle is already on
quests.target: a kettle on the hob
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with the pale window.
It is the second thing on the table, the one first recorded publicly in 1964.
Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose these all are.

ask.question: Covenstead makes a point of what the word rede actually means. What is it?
ask.why: Counsel — the word is Middle English for advice, related to the German Rat. That matters more than it looks: the best-known couplet has been in circulation since it was publicly recorded in 1964 and it has stayed counsel the whole time, rather than hardening into a code somebody can be thrown out for breaking. A great many of us have been handed rules dressed as guidance, and this is the rarer thing running the other way.
hints: It is in the second tenet on the table, and the room repeats it in the section about what is not in the room.
It is a synonym for advice.
The room says the word has stayed this thing for sixty years rather than becoming a commandment.

quests.learned: The best-known line of a living religious tradition is phrased as advice rather than as an order, and has stayed that way — which is a rarer thing than it sounds if you have spent much time being handed rules that were described to you as guidance.

quests.title: The desks are for sitting at
quests.posted: There is a room on this street with the big lights off and the door wedged ajar, where a society of the burnt out meets on the floor. Its standing orders have something to say about the desks. Go and find out who stands on them.
quests.takes: five minutes, lying down if you like
quests.target: a rubber doorstop wedged under the door
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the dark one with a sliver of light in its awning.
The standing orders are near the top of the room, just under the drawing of the doorway.
Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose these are, where the door would swing.

ask.question: Dead Tired Society’s standing orders mention the desks. Who stands on them?
ask.why: Nobody stands on the desks, because most of us have been told to stand up for ourselves quite enough. It is a society of people who are dead tired, and it meets on the floor.
hints: It is in the standing orders, the ones nobody is standing for.
It is the order that mentions standing up for yourself.
One word, meaning no person at all.

quests.learned: A room can make a point of what it will not ask you to do. That one will not ask anybody to stand up — for themselves, for the room, or on a desk — and passing, there, is a whole turn.

quests.title: Who ordered?
quests.posted: There is a comedy club on the street, down a ramp rather than a flight of stairs, where the only thing standing in the spotlight is what the comics said. One of them was at a restaurant when the server asked his friend what he would have. Go and find out what the friend said.
quests.takes: five minutes, or a full hour if you stay for a special
quests.target: a set list taped to the floor of the stage
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with a neon sign in the window.
Josh Blue’s lines are in the spotlight near the top of the room, under his name.
Right at the foot of the room, under the dial, where a set list would be taped down.

ask.question: A server asked Josh Blue’s friend what he would have. The friend guessed Josh would be talking with somebody. Who?
ask.why: “I’m guessing: talk with your manager.” The server had gone round the table taking everybody’s order and, when they got to Josh Blue, asked the person next to him. It is not a rare failure of manners. It is the routine assumption that a disabled person at the table is not the one to address.
hints: It is one of the lines standing in the light, under Josh Blue’s name.
It is the line his friend says, not the one he does.
Whoever you ask for when the service has gone wrong.

quests.learned: Talk to the comic, not to whoever came in with them — which is one of that club’s house rules, and a good one for anywhere with tables in it.

quests.title: Where the attention goes
quests.posted: There is a picture house on the street where the house lights never go down, and one of the films on its rack draws autistic attention as something out in space. Go and find out what.
quests.takes: five minutes, or four more if you watch the film
quests.target: a pair of ear defenders left on a seat
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with a row of warm bulbs in its awning.
It is on the first rack, between Screen One and Screen Two, and the film is the one about monotropism.
Right at the foot of the picture house, under the dial, where somebody left them on a seat.

ask.question: The monotropism film on the rack says focused autistic attention is like something in space, with a pull you cannot easily get out of. What?
ask.why: In the monotropism film, the focus of autistic attention has more mass than anything else around it, and its gravity drags you in. Coming back out of a gravity well takes time, and being pulled out too fast is what gets mistaken for challenging behaviour.
hints: It is on the card for the monotropism film, and in the film itself.
The card calls it a gravity well.
Two words; nothing escapes one.

quests.learned: Attention that goes deep takes time to come back from. That is monotropism, and it is why a relaxed screening lets you walk in late and leave early.

quests.title: Same again
quests.posted: There is a café on the street whose kitchen knows its regulars, and whose specials line says what today’s special is — for everybody who walks in. Go and read it.
quests.takes: as long as a cup of coffee, the same cup as last time
quests.target: a little plastic grass divider, dropped from a tray
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the pale one whose awning is a tray of little wells.
The specials line is right under the café’s name, above the drawing of the table.
Right at the foot of the café, under the section about whose these are, where something slipped off a tray.

ask.question: Samefood Cafe’s specials line says what today’s special is. What is it?
ask.why: Today’s special is your favourite, whoever you are. The kitchen knows its regulars and keeps what each of them has, so the special is never one person’s dish put in front of everybody else — it is the same promise to every guest at once.
hints: It is the line directly under the café’s name.
It is not the same dish for everybody, and it is the same answer for everybody.
Two words: whose, and how much you like it.

quests.learned: A special does not have to be one dish for everybody. A café can default to the same thing every time and still make it a different thing for every guest, because it knows its regulars — and for a great many of us the same again is how eating becomes possible at all.

quests.title: The question nobody asks
quests.posted: There is a dark gallery on the street full of other people’s collections, each under a lamp of its own, and its house rules say there is one question nobody in there will ever ask you about yours. Go and find out which.
quests.takes: as long as it takes to walk past a row of cabinets without counting them
quests.target: a luggage tag that has come off its string
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the dark one whose awning is a row of unlit bays.
The house rules are further down the gallery, after the cabinets.
Right at the foot of the gallery, under the section about whose these are, where a label has come loose.

ask.question: The Collection Collection’s house rules say nobody in there will ask you one question about your collection. What is it? Two words.
ask.why: A collection is not a number, and nothing in that gallery is counted — not the things, not the cabinets. A cabinet with a number beside it has become an inventory.
hints: It is the first of the house rules.
It is the question everybody asks the moment they see a shelf of anything.
Two words, and the answer to it would be a number.

quests.learned: A collection does not have to be counted to count. The gallery shows what people keep, lit the way they choose, with no totals, no prices and no ranking — because a number beside somebody’s things turns something they love into an inventory.

quests.title: Say it plainly
quests.posted: There is a kitchen on the street whose name over the door is a translation, and the room says so near the top. Go and find out what the old name's first word comes from.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to read a menu board
quests.target: a sprig of cilantro, fallen off the shelf
quests.learned: A name can be a translation and say so. Borrowing a word from somebody's faith for a menu that does not keep it would be a claim about the food; saying what the word means in plain English, and crediting where it came from, is the honest version.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the turmeric one whose awning is a row of pots.
Near the top of the kitchen, under the lede, there is a panel about where its name comes from.
Right at the foot of the kitchen, under the section about whose these are, where something fell off the shelf over the counter.

ask.question: The kitchen was going to be called Ital Plant Livity. Which English word does Ital come from?
ask.why: Ital is vital with the v taken off, so that the word begins with I, which Rastafari speech does to a great many words. The kitchen is not Ital, because it cooks with salt, MSG and things out of packets, so the name over the door says vital in plain English instead.
hints: It is in the panel headed where the name comes from.
It is also the first word of the name over the door.
Take one letter off the front of it and you have Ital.

quests.title: What the rocks give back
quests.posted: Third turning off the road out of town there is an open-air stage with something enormous on either side of it, and a lighting rig that points the wrong way. The rocks glow after dark. Go and find out what is actually doing the glowing, and which half of that story the room admits it made up.
quests.takes: ten minutes to read, or nine hours if you press everything
quests.target: a flood lamp at the foot of the rock
hints: Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the third turning.
It is in the section about what the rocks are, in the paragraph that begins by saying which half is real.
Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose all this is.

ask.question: The rocks at Looming Rocks glow under the UV floods, and the room is careful that the stone itself is not what glows. What is?
ask.why: The lichen. Many lichens fluoresce under ultraviolet light — they take light you cannot see and give back light you can — and it is a real technique for telling species apart in the field. The rig, the solar array and the sentient rocks are this street's invention; the fluorescence is not. The room separates those two halves in the same paragraph, and its tool refuses to name any particular species, because nobody here has checked which one glows what and a confident Latin name beside a colour is the format most likely to be believed.
hints: It is not the stone and it is not paint. It is alive, and it is growing on the rock.
It is the thing a walker would call a crust or a patch on a boulder.
Fungus and alga living as one organism.

quests.learned: A real property of a living thing is doing the work that looks most like special effects — and the room is careful to say which half of its own story is invented, which is the same care the herbarium two areas over takes about naming a plant.

quests.title: Who holds the volume
quests.posted: Fourth turning off the road out of town there is a crowd dancing on an old airstrip, and not one sound of it reaches the verge. Go and find out who decides how loud it is.
quests.takes: ten minutes, and nothing plays unless you put a headset on
quests.target: a glow stick snapped and dropped on the runway
hints: Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the fourth turning.
It is in the section about why the room is silent, near the top.
Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is.

ask.question: At Dance, Punks nobody can make anybody else's night louder. Who holds the volume?
ask.why: The dancer. A silent disco hands everybody their own music, on their own headset, at their own volume, so the crowd is still a crowd and the sound only goes where somebody asked for it. That is the dial this whole street runs on, built as a venue: out there, how loud it gets is something the dancer holds rather than a property of the room.
hints: It is not the DJ. There is not one.
It is whoever has the headset on.
The room says loudness is something this person holds rather than a property of the room.

quests.learned: A loud room is an access barrier, and one way round it is to give every person in the crowd their own volume — which is what the dial on every page here is for, too.

quests.title: What the clock is missing
quests.posted: Fifth turning off the road out of town there is a diner with every light on, at an hour when everything else is shut. Something is missing from the clock over its counter. Go and find out what, and why nobody in there minds.
quests.takes: ten minutes, and there is nothing to press
quests.target: a crayon dropped by the door
hints: Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the fifth turning.
It is in the heading of the first window you come to.
Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is.

ask.question: The clock over the counter at The Small Hours is missing something. What?
ask.why: Its hands. The clock over the counter has none, because nobody in there is late and nobody is early — the room's picture of crip time, which Alison Kafer puts as bending the clock to meet disabled bodies and minds rather than the other way round.
hints: It is in the heading of the first window.
A clock needs these to tell anybody anything.
Most clocks have two of them, one long and one short.

quests.learned: Crip time bends the clock to meet the body rather than the body to meet the clock — and some of us are simply awake when the town is not.

quests.title: What a repeater does
quests.posted: Sixth turning off the road out of town, a track goes up to a ridge with a mast on it and nothing lit but two red lamps. Go and find out what the thing on the ridge does with a signal it hears.
quests.takes: ten minutes, or as long as you like with the line open
quests.target: a confirmation card blown against the foot of the mast
hints: Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the sixth turning, and up the track.
It is in the second paragraph at the top of the room.
Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is.

ask.question: The Repeater says what a repeater does with a signal it hears on one frequency. What does it do with it?
ask.why: It passes it on. A repeater listens on one frequency and sends what it hears straight back out on another, louder and from higher up, so that two people who could never reach each other directly can talk — which is why it stands where nobody lives: that is where it can hear everybody. Far off is not the same as cut off.
hints: It is in the paragraph that says what a repeater is.
It sends it back out again — so what does it do with it?
Three words, and the last one is on.

quests.learned: Far off is not the same as cut off. Signal is a mode of connection in its own right, and no mode sits at the top.

quests.title: Not charity
quests.posted: Seventh turning off the road out of town there is a lay-by with a ring of cars in it, headlights on, and tables in the middle with everything on them free. Go and find out what the room says it is instead of.
quests.takes: ten minutes, and there is nothing to press
quests.target: a spare torch left on a tailgate
hints: Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the seventh turning.
It is the first heading in the room.
Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is.

ask.question: Nothing For Sale's first heading is a phrase of the mutual aid movement's: solidarity, not what?
ask.why: Charity. Solidarity, not charity: charity comes down from somebody who has to somebody judged to deserve it, and mutual aid goes sideways, with no proof of worthiness required. That is the whole of the lay-by, and it is why nobody there asks what you need anything for.
hints: It is the first heading in the room.
It is the thing that comes down from above and wants to know you deserve it.
Seven letters, and it begins with a C.

quests.learned: Mutual aid goes sideways and charity comes down. Solidarity, not charity, and no proof of worthiness required.

quests.title: Under the street
quests.posted: The street has an edge at each end, and a third one that is not at either end: straight down, by the lift by the stoop or the stair beside it. Go down and read the caverns, and find out what is doing the lighting.
quests.takes: five minutes, and there is nothing to press
quests.target: a length of handrail on the cavern floor
hints: It is not on the street and not past either end of it. Look for the way down, under the shopfronts with the other things that are not doors.
The answer is in the list called What is down here, in the item about light.
Right at the foot of the caverns, under the section about where the name comes from.

ask.question: Arlesglad Caverns has one light, and it is very particular about where that light is built. What is it built into?
ask.why: The handrail. The strip runs at hand height along the one route, from the lift to every door, so the rock is lit where the path goes and nowhere else. There is no sky down there and no lamp overhead, which is why the only colour in the passage is the light and every room off it brings its own.
hints: It is in the second item of the list called What is down here.
It is not a lamp and it is not the sky. There is neither down there.
You are holding it.

quests.learned: The street has three edges now and only two of them are at an end of it. The caverns are the one you reach by going down, which is also why the guild's class III names all three rather than growing a fourth class for the one that is underneath.

quests.title: The dark shop
quests.posted: Three floors down in the caverns there is a shop full of glow-in-the-dark toys, every one of them dark until you give it some light. Charge them, and find out which colour lasts longest.
quests.takes: five minutes, and a toy or two to hold up to the rail if you want
quests.target: a glow-in-the-dark star, fallen off a ceiling onto the shop floor
hints: It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns and look for level B3.
The answer is in the section called How long a glow lasts.
Right at the foot of the shop, under the credit line.

ask.question: Of every colour glow comes in, which one lasts longest?
ask.why: Green. Green glow pigment is the brightest and longest-lasting there is, and red and orange are the dimmest and first to go, partly because those pigments are weaker and partly because the eye is least sensitive to red in the dark. The shop's own tool refuses a green that does not outlast every other toy on the shelves.
hints: Press Hold everything up to the rail at once, and watch.
It is in the second paragraph of How long a glow lasts.
The colour of the ceiling stars.

quests.learned: A glow-in-the-dark toy does not make light. It keeps some of the light you give it and hands it back, slowly, which is the only light on this street that runs down after you press.

quests.title: Where the knob stops
quests.posted: Out past the last streetlight, an old hangar by the airstrip has the only strobe on the street. Read the walls in the ante-chamber before you go in, and find out how far it goes.
quests.takes: five minutes, and nothing needs switching on
quests.target: a foam earplug, dropped on the hangar floor
hints: It is off The Outskirts, past the last streetlight. Look for turning 08.
The answer is on the strobe and laser warning, in the ante-chamber.
Right at the foot of the hangar, under Whose this all is.

ask.question: The rig's strobe runs from one flash a second up to a number, and the knob stops there on purpose. What number?
ask.why: Eleven. It is a joke about Nigel Tufnel's amplifier in This Is Spinal Tap, and it is also where the knob really ends: the Epilepsy Society puts the flashing most likely to trigger a seizure at 16 to 25 a second, and the room's own tool refuses a knob that goes past eleven. It starts at four, the Health and Safety Executive's recommendation for a club.
hints: It is in the first paragraph of the warning.
It is in the line just under the room's name, too.
Spinal Tap's amplifiers go one louder than ten.

quests.learned: The one room on the street with a strobe in it relaxes a rule by holding the opt-in harder than anywhere else: off on every visit, two presses to start it, and Escape stops everything at once.

quests.title: What the machine takes
quests.posted: Beside the rave's ante-chamber there is a small soft room with a vending machine along one wall. Go and sit down in it for a minute, and find out what the machine takes.
quests.takes: a minute, and a couch
quests.target: a bottle cap, rolled under a couch
hints: It is through the other door in the Rebellion Rave Room's ante-chamber, off The Outskirts.
The answer is in the section called The machine.
Right at the foot of the room, under Whose this all is.

ask.question: What do you have to put into the Cooldown Room's vending machine to get a snack out of it?
ask.why: Nothing. Everything in it is free, you can take as many as you like, and it does not run out and does not ask. The room's own tool will not let a slot carry a price, which is Nothing For Sale's rule arriving on a machine that was built to take money.
hints: Read the sign across the top of the machine.
It is in the first line under The machine.
The same thing Nothing For Sale charges, a few turnings back.

quests.learned: A free vending machine does the one thing it was never built for. Taking from it puts nobody in anybody's debt.

quests.title: The cellar at the top of the lift
quests.posted: One floor down under the street there is a cellar with house styles of beer, wine and kombucha. Read how the pours are set out, and find out which one comes first.
quests.takes: five minutes, and there is nothing to press or to drink
quests.target: a glass carboy standing on the cellar floor
hints: It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns; this is the first level.
The answer is in the introduction to Try our house styles.
Right at the foot of the cellar, under the credit line.

ask.question: Every house style in Big Steep comes as two pours. Which pour always comes first?
ask.why: The alcohol-free one, and at the same size as the other, because it is not the lesser pour. Many people do not drink, for all kinds of reasons and for none, and a cellar that listed that pour second or smaller would be telling them they were an afterthought. The room's own tool refuses a house style whose first pour has alcohol in it.
hints: It is in the sentence in bold just under Try our house styles.
Look at the two boxes under any house style, and read the left one.
The one without.

quests.learned: Every pour on this street says how strong it is before you take it, the same way every button says how long it runs before you press it. The number is what lets somebody decide.

quests.title: The farm under the street
quests.posted: Two floors down in the caverns there is a mushroom farm with a restaurant at the end of it. Read why it is there, and find out what happens to the blocks the mushrooms grew on once they are finished.
quests.takes: five minutes, and there is nothing to press
quests.target: a spent growing block on the kitchen floor
hints: It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns and look for level B2.
The answer is in the section called Why a mushroom farm.
Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line.

ask.question: When a block of straw or sawdust has given all the mushrooms it is going to, what does it go out of the farm as?
ask.why: Compost. The mushroom is only the fruit; the mycelium is the part that grew all the way through the block, and when it is spent the block goes back out as compost. Which is the line of ours the room is built on: composting is not destruction, it is how a commons renews itself.
hints: It is in the paragraph after the quotation.
Our own line about it is quoted just above.
It goes back to the soil.

quests.learned: A mushroom is the fruit and not the thing that grows. The part doing the work is the mycelium, the part nobody sees on a plate, which is a fair description of most of the work on this street.

quests.title: The bottom of the caverns
quests.posted: Go all the way down: past every level of the caverns to the one at the bottom, where the temperature stops moving. Read the room's rules, and find out what the dial on the page does down there.
quests.takes: five minutes, and there is nothing to press
quests.target: a thermometer lying on the floor
hints: It is under the street. Take the lift by the stoop down to the caverns, and then go to the bottom of its panel.
The answer is in the list called What never changes in here.
Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line.

ask.question: Every page on this street has a dial that turns the motion and sparkle up and down. What does it change in Stay Frosty?
ask.why: Nothing. The dial still works on that page, and it has nothing to change there, because nothing in the room moves at any setting. That is a sentence on the page, so the room's own tool refuses an animation, a transition or a transform in its stylesheet rather than trusting the dial to reset one.
hints: It is in the second item of the list called What never changes in here.
The dial works. The question is what it finds to do.
Nothing moves in that room.

quests.learned: The dial is the street's promise that loudness is yours to hold. In a room with nothing loud in it, the promise is kept by there being nothing to turn down, which is the one setting where Gentle, Regular and MAX look exactly the same.

quests.title: Behind the quiet room
quests.posted: At the very bottom of the caverns there is a room where nothing moves, and a door at the back of it. Go through, and read the house rules of the room full of fans.
quests.takes: five minutes, and you can do it without switching a single fan on
quests.target: a ribbon off a fan's cage, lying on the floor
hints: It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns, go to the bottom, and look for the door at the back of the quiet room.
The answer is in the house rules, in the one about the ceiling fans.
Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line.

ask.question: Every ceiling fan in Stay Breezy has its lamp hung in one particular place, so that nothing in the room flickers. Where is the lamp?
ask.why: Below the blades. A lamp above turning blades throws a flickering shadow onto everything under it, which on this street is a strobe arriving through a light fitting. So every ceiling fan's lamp hangs under its hub, and the room's own tool checks the drawings to make sure.
hints: It is in the house rules, the second one.
Think about which side of the blades the light has to be on for them never to cut across it.
Not above.

quests.learned: The loudest room in the caverns and the quietest one share a wall, and both keep the same promise from opposite ends: nothing flashes, and nothing happens to you that you did not switch on.

quests.title: The door the radio waits outside
quests.posted: There is a radio on this street that follows you from room to room once you have switched it on. There is one door it will not go through. Find out which, and why.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to read a noticeboard
quests.target: a push-in letter, fallen off the letterboard
quests.learned: A room's promise about itself holds even against the street's own furniture. The Healing Checkpoint says it writes nothing down about you, so the radio that remembers where you put it waits outside, rather than the room's promise being quietly narrowed to fit the radio.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the powder-blue one with its blinds half down.
Inside, under the front desk, there is a list of how the radio works. The last thing on it is a room.
Right at the foot of the hall, under the section about whose this is, where something fell off the letterboard.

ask.question: Which room does the CB's radio stay out of?
ask.why: Room 429 promises that it writes nothing down about you and has no fetch in it. The radio listens to a server and remembers where you put it, so it would make that promise untrue, and it waits outside the door instead.
hints: It is the last thing in the list headed How the radio works.
It is a guest room with a bed nobody is charging you for.
Its room number is 429.

quests.title: What the middle of the building is open to
quests.posted: There is a town hall on the street, a round hall with rooms off it. Go in and find out what the top of its dome is open to.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to look up
quests.target: a gavel, left on the floor of the rotunda
quests.learned: A private room and a public record are two different things, and a building can have a place for each: doors round the wall for what has to stay in the room, and the middle open to the sky.
hints: On the street, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a round hole in its roof.
Read the lede, and the section headed Why a hole in the roof.
The gavel is on the floor at the foot of the hall, before the sign-off.

ask.question: What is the top of the Town Hall's dome open to?
ask.why: The top of the dome is a round hole, open to the sky, and the sun comes through it and lies on the floor as one disc. The rooms round the wall have doors; the middle of the building has none.
hints: Look at the top of the drawing.
It is round and there is no glass in it.
What is above a roof with a hole in it?

quests.title: The seat nobody sits in
quests.posted: Through a door off the Town Hall there is a fishbowl on a sunny sill. Go and find out what the circle in the middle always keeps.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to feed a fish
quests.target: a flake of fish food, fallen on the sill
quests.learned: A conversation stays open when there is always room to come in. The fishbowl keeps one seat in the middle empty, and whoever takes it is joined by somebody else stepping back out.
hints: Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Fishbowl's door.
Read How a fishbowl goes.
The flake is on the sill at the foot of the room, before the sign-off.

ask.question: What does the middle of a fishbowl always keep?
ask.why: One seat in the middle is always left empty, so anybody from the outer circle can come in and take it; when they do, somebody in the middle goes back out.
hints: It is in the first paragraph of How a fishbowl goes.
Look at the ring of stones in the bowl.
Nobody is sitting in it.

quests.title: How the light gets in
quests.posted: Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' directors, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what the light comes through.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to read a name backwards
quests.target: a key, left on the floor inside the door
quests.learned: A room can be private without being hidden. The door is not locked, the directors' names are on the wall, and the glass lets the light through while keeping the detail back.
hints: Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Directors' door.
Read Why frosted glass.
The key is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off.

ask.question: What does the light in the Directors' room come through?
accept: the frosted glass in the door
ask.why: There is no lamp in the room: the only light is the hall's, through the frosted pane in the door, so it comes in soft and without an edge, and the name on the glass reads backwards from inside.
hints: There is no lamp in the room.
Look at the door in the drawing.
It lets light through and keeps the detail back.

quests.title: Whose lamp is biggest
quests.posted: Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' board, at one long table. Go and find out what every seat at it has in front of it.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to count down a table
quests.target: a pencil, rolled off the table
quests.learned: A board is a table where every seat counts the same. Nobody's lamp is bigger, and there is no light over the head of the table.
hints: Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Board's door.
Read Why a lamp at every seat.
The pencil is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off.

ask.question: What does every seat at the Board's table have in front of it?
ask.why: Every seat has the same small shaded lamp and the same pool of light in front of it, down both sides, and nobody's lamp is bigger: a board is a table where every seat counts the same.
hints: There is no light over the head of the table.
Look at the drawing, down both sides.
It is small and shaded, and it is the same at every seat.

quests.title: What lights the room that looks after the street
quests.posted: Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' moderators, above the street at night, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what it is lit by.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to look at a ceiling
quests.target: a spare fuse, left on the windowsill
quests.learned: The room that looks after the street is lit by the street: every shopfront's colour comes up through its window and lies on the ceiling beside the others, none mixed into the next.
hints: Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Moderators' door.
Read Why the street's own light.
The fuse is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off.

ask.question: What lights the Moderators' room?
ask.why: There is no lamp in the room: the shopfronts below throw their own colours up through the window, and they lie on the ceiling side by side.
hints: There is no lamp in the room.
Look at the ceiling in the drawing, and at what is under the window.
The room is up above it.

quests.title: The one light left on
quests.posted: Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room where the board meets without staff, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what the one light in it is.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to read a sign
quests.target: a folded note, left on a chair
quests.learned: An executive session is the board meeting without staff, and a board that holds one at every meeting never has to mean anything by holding one.
hints: Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Executive Session door.
Read Why an exit sign.
The note is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off.

ask.question: What is the only light in the Executive Session room?
ask.why: There is no lamp: the one light is the EXIT sign over the shut door, left on once everybody who is not on the board has gone out through it.
hints: There is no lamp in the room.
Look over the door in the drawing.
It is green, and it says the way out.

quests.title: Black is a colour
quests.posted: There is a shop on the street for dressing in whatever makes you glad to have it on. Go and find out which colour every rail in it comes in, whatever else it comes in.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to try something on
quests.target: a feather, come off the boa, on the floor
quests.learned: Dopamine dressing is not the same as wearing colour. It is wearing what makes you glad to have it on, and for a great many people that is black. A room that told them colour was what they needed would be a dress code with a nicer name.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the lavender one with a strip of patchwork for an awning.
Under the stand and the looks off the peg there are house rules, and the first one is about dress codes.
Right at the foot of the shop, under the section about whose this is, where something fell off the boa.

ask.question: Every rail in the Dress-Up Den comes in one colour, whatever else it comes in. Which colour?
ask.why: Black is a colour in there. Our Dress Codes entry has a school that banned black clothing on the grounds of mental health, and a room that said colour was the cure would be that dress code with a nicer name. So every rail comes in all black, and choosing it is as much dopamine dressing as choosing all the colours there are.
hints: It is in the first of the house rules.
It is also the last colourway in every colours list on the rails.
A school in our Dress Codes entry banned clothes in it.

quests.title: Nobody is bigger than anybody
quests.posted: There is a poster pasted round a column out on the pavement, saying what every room on the street puts on first. Go and read it, and find out the one thing every other gig poster has that this one will not print.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to read a bill standing on a pavement
quests.target: the paste brush the bill went up with, left on the pavement at the foot of the column
quests.learned: The poster belongs to all of those rooms at once, so every name on it is set the same size and they run in the order you would walk to them. A gig poster that put one of them in big letters at the top would be ranking our own rooms against each other, on a sheet none of them chose.
hints: On the pavement beside the Pebble Board, on a column of its own rather than behind the glass.
Under the bill, where the poster says how it is printed.
At the foot of the column, on the pavement, where the paste brush was put down.

ask.question: Most gig posters print one act bigger than all the others, at the top. What does this poster have no room for?
ask.why: There is no headliner. Every room's name is the same size, in the order you would reach them walking down the street, because a poster that belongs to every room cannot make one of them the draw.
hints: It is in the line just above the bill.
It is also in how the poster is printed, in the third rule.
It is the word for the act a gig poster is built around.

quests.title: When does the wall repaint itself?
quests.posted: There is an end wall on the street that will not stay one colour. Go and stand across the road from it, and find out when it repaints itself without anybody asking.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to watch a wall, which is not as long as you would think
quests.target: the lid off a tin of paint, left on the pavement with a ring of yellow dried round it
quests.learned: A picture that changes without being asked is something moving on the page, so the wall only turns over by itself at MAX GLITTER. At Gentle and Regular it holds still until you turn it over, and every mural is in words under it at every setting, because the dial takes away the wobble and never the words.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a strip of fresh paint under its capping.
Under the list of murals, where the room says how the wall works.
At the foot of the wall, on the pavement, where somebody put the lid down.

ask.question: The wall repaints itself at one setting of the dial and holds still at the other two. Which setting?
ask.why: Only at MAX GLITTER does anything on this street move without being asked. At Gentle and Regular the wall waits for you to turn it over, and the list under it holds every mural in words at every setting.
hints: It is in the first of the rules about how the wall works.
The hold button only appears at that setting.
It is the loudest of the three.

quests.title: What are you, at the library?
quests.posted: There is a public library on the street with the sky in its windows, and somebody has left a book on the floor with its date-due slip sticking out. Go and read the room, and find out what the library says you are when you walk in.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to read a reading room's notices, and you can sit down
quests.target: a returned book lying on the floor, its date-due slip sticking out of the top
quests.learned: At the library you are a patron, not a customer. Nothing requires a card, you do not have to buy anything to be there, and nobody checks whether you are being social correctly. That is what makes a library a third place.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with sky in its windows.
In the first paragraph under the drawing of the reading room, and again in the praise of the public library.
On the floor at the foot of the room, under the last notice, where somebody put a book down.

ask.question: At the library, you are a patron and not a what?
ask.why: The library says it twice: at the library you are a patron, not a customer. Nothing there requires a card, and nobody asks you to buy anything to justify being in the room.
hints: It is in bold at the end of the paragraph under the drawing.
It is the word for somebody a shop wants money from.
Cory Doctorow's line uses it too.

quests.title: What do you need to find your way through L-space?
quests.posted: There is a gap in the stacks at the back of the Community Library that is longer on the inside than it is on the outside. Go down it, and find out what you need to find your way back.
quests.takes: one gap in the stacks, and as long in there as you like, which is never as long as it felt
quests.target: the loose end of a ball of string, coiled on the floor where it was tied off
quests.learned: In L-space what you need is not a map but a ball of string, because nothing in there is straight. Tie one end to the door you came in by and follow the thread: that is how we think about a library, and how a monotropic mind walks one anyway.
hints: Through the gap in the stacks at the back of the Community Library.
In the first paragraph under the drawing, and again in Terry Pratchett's own words further down.
On the floor at the foot of the room, where the string was tied off.

ask.question: When you set out to look something up in the folds of L-space, what do you really need?
ask.why: Nothing in L-space is straight, so a map would be no use. Pratchett's answer, in Guards! Guards!, is a ball of string: tie it to the door and follow it back.
hints: It is not a map.
It is drawn right across the top of the room.
You tie one end to the door.

quests.title: Why did the Librarian keep his job?
quests.posted: At the far end of the string in L-space somebody has tied it round a banana, and on the other side of the shelf there is a room in the Librarian's own colours. Go and find out why he kept his job when everything else about him changed.
quests.takes: the length of a ball of string, and one room at the end of it
quests.target: a banana skin on the floor, left where somebody finished the banana
quests.learned: The Librarian kept his job because he was the only one who knew where all the books were. His body changed by accident, he found the new one suited the work, and he declined to be changed back; being the expert is a reason to keep a job that an institution cannot argue with.
hints: Through the Community Library's gap in the stacks, and all the way along the string in L-space to the end.
In the first paragraph under the drawing of the Disc, and again under why we find him relatable.
On the floor at the foot of the room, where somebody dropped a banana skin.

ask.question: The Librarian kept his job because he was the only one who knew where all the what were?
ask.why: He was the only one who knew where all the books were, so however the University felt about an orangutan in the stacks, the matter was never really raised.
hints: It is in the first paragraph under the drawing.
A library is full of them.
He climbs the shelves to reach them.

quests.title: Who signed for his own books?
quests.posted: There is a house on the street, green throughout, with a shut door onto each of our calls and not one of them locked. Go in, do not open a door, and find out what the man it is named after signed every time he took a book out of his own library.
quests.takes: about as long as reading one paragraph, and no call to join
quests.target: a folded note left on the hall floor, with a round seal on it
quests.learned: Henry Cavendish opened his library in Bedford Square for borrowing and signed its register for every book he took, like anybody else. A house can be open without being open-plan: what makes it open is that anybody can find out what is behind each door and when, that the rules apply to the people who run it, and that nothing is locked.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with its blinds down.
In the part of the room about the house in Bedford Square.
At the foot of the room, on the hall floor, where somebody left a note.

ask.question: Every time Henry Cavendish took a book out of his own library, he signed something, like anybody else. What?
ask.why: The library in Bedford Square had rules, and the rules were his too: he signed its register for every book he took to his other house at Clapham. That is the room's idea of open: the rules on the door apply to the people who run the house.
hints: It is in the part of the room about the house in Bedford Square.
It is the book a library keeps of what has gone out.
One word, and it is also what you do when you sign in somewhere.

On the desk, in the Austin City Limits section.

ask.question: One session on the desk was taped on a night most people know by name. Which night?

quests.title: Whose street is it?
quests.posted: There is a ship on the street with its ports open and a sheet of paper in every one where a gun would be. Go alongside, turn the first sheet over, and find out who the street is named after.
quests.takes: about as long as reading one side of one sheet, and nothing to print
quests.target: a sheet that came down in the bottom of your boat
quests.learned: The street is Danny the Street's: a living street in DC Comics' Doom Patrol, created in 1990 by Grant Morrison and Richard Case, who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter. Side B of the first sheet says so on the paper, because a printed sheet is the one place a credit cannot be a link somebody follows later.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one that is the side of a ship.
On side B of the first sheet on the press.
At the foot of the room, where a sheet came down in the bottom of your boat.

ask.question: Side B of No. 1 says the street has a name and that it is not ours. Whose name is it?
ask.why: The street is named after Danny the Street, a living street in DC Comics' Doom Patrol, created in 1990 by Grant Morrison and Richard Case. Side B of the first sheet says so on the paper, because a printed sheet is the one place a credit cannot be a link somebody follows later.
hints: It is on side B of No. 1, under Where the street came from.
A character in DC Comics' Doom Patrol.
A living street, and a first name you have heard before.

quests.title: What flavour is Thursday?
quests.posted: There is an ice cream parlour on the street that stays lit after closing, with the news of every morning of the week in its cabinet, a tub to a morning. Go in and find out what flavour Thursday comes in.
quests.takes: about as long as reading the lids in the cabinet, and nothing to play
quests.target: an ice cream scoop dropped on the floor by the cabinet, with some mint still in it
quests.learned: Every morning's tub in the cabinet is a flavour, and the flavour is the day of the week, so Thursday is always vanilla whatever is in it. How far down a tub is scraped says how many mornings old it is, and after a week it is gone.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a row of ice cream tubs in its awning.
In the cabinet: every tub's lid names its day and its flavour.
At the foot of the room, on the floor in front of the cabinet, where somebody dropped the scoop.

ask.question: Every tub in the cabinet is a morning, and every morning is a flavour. What flavour is Thursday?
ask.why: Every morning's tub in the cabinet is a flavour, and the flavour is the day of the week, so Thursday is always vanilla whatever is in it. How far down a tub is scraped says how many mornings old it is, and after a week it is gone.
hints: Every tub's lid says its day and its flavour, right under the date.
Find the tub whose date is a Thursday; there is always exactly one in a week.
The plainest flavour there is.

quests.posted: There is a boot room on the street with a whole estuary out of its back door, and the tide out there does not keep time. Go and find out what turns it.
quests.takes: a walk down the street, and a look out the back door

ask.question: On the Slake, out the back door of the MUD Room, what makes the tide turn?
ask.why: Waiting for it. Nothing on the Slake runs on a clock: the tide is in or out until you say wait, somewhere dry, and then it turns. That is the street's oldest promise, that nothing moves until you say so, made into weather.
hints: Read the noticeboard in the MUD Room itself.

quests.learned: A world can wait for you. Nothing on the Slake changes until you ask it to.

quests.title: How often will the tree take water?
quests.posted: There is a tree on a hillside behind the shopfronts that is everybody's, and it grows as we water it. Go up the hill and find out how often the ground will take another watering.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes a watering to soak in
quests.target: a gold aspen leaf, fallen at the foot of the fence round the new growth
quests.learned: The ground soaks for a minute after every watering, from anybody, before it takes more. It is the whole tree's wait and not anybody's, so nobody is timed, and the tree keeps how many times it has been watered and never who watered it.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the gap with a hillside of aspen in it.
Under the grove, where the room says how the tree grows.
At the foot of the fence, where the leaves come down.

ask.question: After every watering the ground soaks for a while before it will take more. How long?
ask.why: The ground soaks for a minute after anybody's watering. It is the whole tree's wait rather than yours, which is how the tree can wait without keeping a record of who watered it.
hints: It is in the rules about how the tree grows.
It is the same wait for everybody.
It is sixty seconds.

quests.title: How many words in a row can one person put up?
quests.posted: There is a kitchen on the street with a fridge door covered in word magnets, and a sentence on it that everybody is writing together. Go and read the door, and find out how many words anybody can put up in a row.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes somebody else to put up the next word
quests.target: a word magnet that has slid to the foot of the fridge door, with nothing on it yet
quests.learned: One word each, and never two in a row: once you have put one up, the next is somebody else's. The fridge keeps a scrambled mark of whoever put up the last word, only so it can keep that rule, and the next word replaces it; nothing says whose any word was.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a chrome handle down its awning.
In the rules about how the door works.
At the foot of the door, where a magnet ends up when it slides.

ask.question: Once you have put up a word, how many more can you put up before somebody else puts up one?
ask.why: Nobody puts up two words in a row, so after your word the next one is somebody else's. After theirs you can go again.
hints: It is the first rule about how the door works.
The next word is always somebody else's.
Not a single one.

quests.title: How far does the lift take you?
quests.posted: There is a stairwell on the street that everybody climbs together, a number to a step, and a chairlift on its wall. Go through the fire door and find out how far the lift takes you.
quests.takes: about as long as one step
quests.target: the stairlift's call button, a small box on the wall at the foot of the stairs
quests.learned: The lift takes you up one step and counts exactly the same as a number, and it can never send the stair back to one, because it asks the stair for the next step rather than guessing it. Nothing says which way anybody came up.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the fire door with the stair's nosings on its awning.
Where the stair gives you two ways up.
At the foot of the stairs, on the wall, where you would call the lift.

ask.question: How many steps does one ride on the lift take you up?

hints: It is in the box that says By the lift.
It is the same as one number.
A single step.

quests.title: Where does an adopted cat go?

hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the dark one with two eyes on its awning.
In the rules about how rescuing and adopting work.
On the kerb, where somebody put the torch down.

ask.question: When you adopt a cat, where on your CB radio do they go?

quests.title: What does Forget Me forget?
quests.posted: There is a park on the street the morning after snow, where dogs turn up who need bringing in, and anybody signed on can adopt one into the Pets tray on their CB. The tray has a Forget Me in it. Go and find out what it forgets.
quests.takes: about as long as it takes to follow a line of prints
quests.target: a dog's red lead, dropped in the snow by a gate, with prints going off from it
quests.learned: Forget Me deletes everything the street keeps under your handle, which is your pets, and the animals stay on the list of everybody adopted, where nothing ever connected them to you. A handle is not an account, so anybody who signs on with yours sees the same pets.
hints: On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the white one with paw prints across its awning.
In the rules about how rescuing and adopting work.
In the snow by the gate, where somebody let go of the lead.

_where: EVERY MARKER IS ON THE FLOOR OF ITS ROOM, which on a web page means the bottom of it, and the guild says so out loud. Scattering them at a different depth in every room would have been more like a hunt and would have made finding one a test of eyesight and of a mouse -- on a Disabled people's site, where the hunt is meant to be the walk between rooms rather than the search within one. So the hints name the ROOM, the class says how far the walk is, and the last hint says where on the floor. What is never the same twice is the marker itself: one drawing per room, in that room's own colours, refused by make-guild.py if a room has none.
